title: PJM Capacity Auction Procures 138,318 MW of Generation Resources as Work Continues To Address Growing Electricity Demand
date_evidence: (Valley Forge, PA – July 14, 2026) – PJM Interconnection today announced the results of its 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction
key_claim: The 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction cleared at the FERC-approved cap of $325/MW-day and left committed supply 6,831 MW short of the reliability requirement, the second consecutive RTO-wide shortfall; PJM plans a September Backstop Procurement.
frame_summary: PJM argues that demand keeps growing faster than supply and presents the capped price and reliability shortfall as manageable through a portfolio of interconnection, backstop-procurement and flexible-load measures rather than as market failure.
verbatim_quote: The price came in at the FERC-approved cap, $325/MW-day (UCAP) for the entire PJM footprint, a 2.5% decrease from the 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction cap of $333.44/MW-day.
verbatim_list: PJM Interconnection today announced the results of its 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, which secured 138,318 MW of unforced capacity generation (UCAP) and demand response to meet projected electricity needs for more than 67 million people
The capacity of the resources procured in the auction, plus FRR resources, is short of PJM’s reliability requirement by 6,831 MW
The cleared supply procured in the auction times the clearing price totals $16.4 billion.
PJM continues to hold a reserve margin of 14.7% for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.

These most recent auctions were the first in PJM history in which the entire RTO fell short of the reliability requirement. PJM plans to seek FERC approval to hold a special “Backstop Procurement” in September
including a shortfall of approximately 6,500 MW in the previous capacity auction (for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year)
The supply mix for RPM cleared and FRR committed resources in this auction in UCAP includes: 46% natural gas, 20% nuclear, 18% coal, 5% demand response, 4% hydro, 2% wind, 2% oil and 1% solar.

title: 2026 DOE 202(c) Orders
key_claim: DOE's 2026 Section 202(c) log now runs to Order No. 202-26-36, with heat-driven emergency orders to PJM (14 July) and SPP (20 July) and seasonal orders keeping coal and oil units at Campbell, Eddystone, Wagner, Culley, Schahfer, Centralia, Craig and Stanton available into August and September 2026.
frame_summary: The DOE log presents Section 202(c) emergency authority as a standing reliability instrument, framing each order as a response to anticipated supply shortfalls rather than as intervention in state resource planning.
verbatim_quote: The order directs SPP to dispatch specified units and to order their operation as needed to maintain reliability.
verbatim_list: The order also authorizes SPP to direct backup generation resources to operate as a last resort before declaring an Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) 3 or during an EEA 3.

The order directs MISO to ensure that the J.H. Campbell coal-fired power plant in West Olive, Michigan remains available to operate and to employ economic dispatch to minimize costs for the American people. This order is in effect beginning on May 19, 2026 and continues until August 16, 2026.

title: NOAA predicts below-normal 2026 Atlantic hurricane season
key_claim: NOAA's outlook predicts a 55% chance of a below-normal 2026 Atlantic season with 8-14 named storms, 3-6 hurricanes and 1-3 major hurricanes, as El Nino is expected to develop and intensify.
frame_summary: NOAA argues the season will most likely be below normal because of a developing El Nino, while insisting that preparedness matters regardless because it only takes one landfalling storm to make a bad season.
verbatim_quote: NOAA’s outlook for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, which runs June 1 to November 30, predicts a 35% chance of a near-normal season, a 10% chance of an above-normal season, and a 55% chance of a below-normal season.
verbatim_list: The agency is forecasting a total of 8-14 named storms (winds of 39 mph or higher). Of those, 3-6 are forecast to become hurricanes (winds of 74 mph or higher), including 1-3 major hurricanes (category 3, 4 or 5 with winds of 111 mph or higher).

“Although El Niño’s impact in the Atlantic Basin can often suppress hurricane development, there is still uncertainty in how each season will unfold,” said NOAA’s National Weather Service Director Ken Graham.
It only takes one storm to make for a very bad season.

title: Canicule : la sécurité d'approvisionnement en électricité n'appelle aucune vigilance particulière

title: Electricity 2026 - Executive summary
date_evidence: IEA 2026 electricity report: global electricity demand rises with cooling among key growth drivers | 2026/02/25 (iifiir.org search-result snippet dating the Electricity 2026 release; IEA event page confirms the report was 'published in February')
key_claim: Global electricity demand is forecast to grow 3.6% a year over 2026-2030 while more than 2,500 GW of projects sit stalled in grid connection queues; grid investment needs to rise roughly 50% from today's USD 400 billion, and flexible connections plus grid-enhancing technologies could unlock 1,200-1,600 GW.
frame_summary: The IEA argues the binding problem of the Age of Electricity is no longer generation but grids and flexibility, and that regulatory reform and non-firm connections can unlock large stranded queue capacity faster than physical build-out alone.
verbatim_quote: Global electricity demand is forecast to increase at a brisk average annual rate of 3.6% over the 2026-2030 forecast period, supported by rising consumption from industry, electric vehicles, air conditioning and data centres.
verbatim_list: more than 2 500 gigawatts (GW) worth of projects – encompassing renewables, storage, and projects with large loads, such as data centres − remain stalled in grid connection queues worldwide
Meeting forecasted electricity demand through 2030 would require annual grid investment to increase by roughly 50% by 2030 from today’s USD 400 billion
these measures together could free up enough capacity to connect around 1 200 GW to 1 600 GW of advanced‑stage projects currently stuck in queues worldwide
About 750 GW to 900 GW of projects could be enabled via more flexible, non-firm grid connection agreements.

In the United States, electricity demand rose by 2.1% in 2025 and is projected to grow by nearly 2% annually through 2030, with around half of the total increase driven by the rapid expansion of data centres.

title: European integrated framework for climate resilience
key_claim: The Commission's integrated framework for climate resilience is planned for adoption in Q4 2026, built around a common 3°C reference scenario, risk ownership and resilience-by-design, with only 25% of climate-related losses in Europe currently insured.
frame_summary: The Parliament's tracker argues the EU is moving climate resilience from voluntary adaptation planning to a binding, harmonised risk-management regime with clearly assigned responsibilities and attention to the insurance protection gap.
verbatim_quote: The Commission adoption is planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.
verbatim_list: Particular attention would be given to addressing the finance and insurance protection gaps, noting that only 25 % of climate-related losses in Europe are currently insured.
The first European climate risk assessment identifies 36 climate risks that threaten Europe’s ecosystems, populations, and the economy.

title: H1 2026 Gallagher Re Natural Catastrophe and Climate Report
key_claim: H1 2026 natural catastrophes caused USD 142 billion in economic and USD 46 billion in insured losses, both below long-term averages, the lowest first-half insured total since 2019, extending a five-quarter streak without a USD 10 billion-plus insured event as El Nino arrives.
frame_summary: Gallagher Re argues that a benign loss half-year reflects the absence of outsized single events rather than reduced societal risk, and flags El Nino and record European heat as the considerations that should discipline second-half complacency.
verbatim_quote: H1 global natural catastrophe events resulted in USD142 billion in economic losses and USD46 billion in insured losses, both below long-term averages.
verbatim_list: Notably, H1 2026 recorded the lowest first-half economic loss total since 2020 and the lowest first-half insured loss total since 2019.
the absence of a major catastrophe generating more than USD10 billion in insured losses extended a streak of five consecutive quarters without such an event
El Niño conditions have officially arrived, with NOAA indicating at least a 63% chance of "very strong" intensity by year-end.

events such as the catastrophic Venezuela earthquake sequence, record-breaking European heatwaves and widespread severe convective storm activity across North America underscore that below-average industry losses do not necessarily equate to reduced societal risk

date_evidence: Evergreen perspective page with no publication date in page metadata; accessed 2026-07-23. Meta description: 'the launch of the European Commission’s EU Critical Entities Resilience (CER) Directive which Member States will have to adhere to by 17th July 2026.'
notes: publication_date set to access date; page is an undated evergreen perspective. Bibliography renders as accessed date.
key_claim: Under the CER Directive, Member States had to identify and designate critical entities across 11 sectors by 17 July 2026, after which designated entities face binding resilience obligations.
frame_summary: Deloitte argues that recent shocks exposed resilience planning gaps and that the CER Directive converts resilience from a leadership aspiration into a compliance obligation organisations must operationalise now.
verbatim_quote: This has resulted in an urgent imperative to bolster resilience capabilities and the launch of the European Commission’s EU Critical Entities Resilience (CER) Directive which Member States will have to adhere to by 17th July 2026.

title: Powering the US Data Center Boom: Why Forecasting Can Be So Tricky
notes: Structural anchor: canonical explainer of why US data-centre demand forecasts diverge and how phantom load distorts planning; anchors the demand-forecast-scrutiny thread.
key_claim: Modelled US data-centre energy-use projections through 2030 range from 200 TWh/year to over 1,050 TWh/year, and speculative interconnection requests are producing double counting and phantom load that distort utility planning.
frame_summary: WRI argues the real risk is not demand growth itself but planning against wildly uncertain forecasts, so policymakers should demand transparency, uncertainty-aware forecasting and tariffs that stop phantom load costs landing on ordinary ratepayers.
verbatim_quote: Modeled energy use projections through 2030 range from 200 TWh/year to over 1,050 TWh/year.
verbatim_list: this practice is leading to both double counting of projects and “phantom” load that will never be built, distorting load forecasts and utility resource planning processes
Many estimates, however, put data center energy use between 300 TWh/year and 400 TWh/year by 2030

title: CSU Lowers Atlantic Hurricane Forecast to 'Well Below Normal'
key_claim: CSU's 8 July update cut the 2026 Atlantic forecast to nine named storms, four hurricanes and one major hurricane, its third reduction this year, with a 17% chance of a major US landfall versus a 43% historical average.
frame_summary: The report argues a strengthening El Nino will dominate the peak season and make 2026 potentially the quietest hurricane year since 2015, materially lowering but not eliminating US landfall risk.
verbatim_quote: In a July 8 update to its forecast, CSU said the 2026 hurricane season will have nine named storms, four hurricanes, and one major hurricane.
verbatim_list: The latest forecast from CSU gives a 17% chance of a major hurricane making landfall along the U.S. coastline (the average from 1880–2020 is 43%).
Should CSU’s forecast hold up, 2026 would be the quietest season for hurricanes since 2015
An average hurricane season, which runs June 1 to Nov. 30, has about 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes.

title: Data centers have already hiked electricity prices on the public by $23 billion. Good luck clawing that back
notes: Republished from The Conversation; author Theodore J. Kury, University of Florida.
key_claim: PJM's independent market monitor concluded that expected data-centre demand was a primary reason for $23 billion in customer price increases lasting until at least end-2028, and cost-allocation rules give data centres routes to avoid peak-based charges.
frame_summary: The piece argues that ratepayers are structurally under-represented in cost-allocation proceedings, so data-centre-driven infrastructure costs are already shifting onto households and will be hard to claw back if forecast load never materialises.
verbatim_quote: concluded that expected power demand from data centers was a primary reason for $23 billion in customer price increases that will last until at least the end of 2028

title: Europe's extreme heat is shutting down power plants
key_claim: France's hottest day on record since 1947 forced reactor shutdowns and ramp-downs as rivers ran too hot for cooling, five UK gas plants cut about 2.5 GW, and EDF's climate-proofing is costed at about EUR 600 million a year over 15 years.
frame_summary: The article argues extreme heat is now a systemic constraint on thermal generation of every kind, arriving exactly when cooling demand peaks, and that climate-proofing power systems will be expensive and continuous.
verbatim_quote: On June 23, France saw its hottest day since record-keeping began in 1947. Temperatures climbed to over 44 °C (111 °F), and overnight temperatures remained unusually high.
verbatim_list: Five gas plants across the UK have reported output reductions due to the conditions, cutting a total of about 2.5 gigawatts from the power supply.
Upgrades are expected to cost about €600 million per year (about $680 million) over the next 15 years.
At least seven gigawatts’ worth of nuclear energy was forced to shut down across the country during a heat wave in July 2025

title: BloombergNEF forecasts 158GW of global energy storage deployments in 2026
key_claim: BNEF's Energy Storage Outlook H1 2026 counts a record 112 GW / 307 GWh added in 2025 and forecasts 158 GW / 459 GWh in 2026, a 41% increase, with annual additions almost doubling to 308 GW by 2036; the US and China took about 70% of 2025 deployments.
frame_summary: The report argues storage has crossed into industrial maturity, scaling faster than solar or wind did at the same stage and becoming the flexibility backbone of high-renewables systems despite policy churn in its two biggest markets.
verbatim_quote: BNEF launched its Energy Storage Outlook H1 2026 report this week. The market intelligence firm counted 112GW/307GWh of new additions last year, and forecasts 158GW/459GWh of deployments worldwide for 2026.
verbatim_list: After reporting a record 112GW of global non-pumped hydro energy storage installations in 2025, BloombergNEF (BNEF) expects to see a 41% increase this year.
BNEF has predicted that annual additions will almost double over the next 10 years, reaching 308GW by 2036
The world’s two biggest markets by country, the US and China, accounted for around 70% of all 2025 deployments.

title: NERC overstates reliability risks in long-term assessment: Grid Strategies
key_claim: Grid Strategies' March 2026 report argues NERC's long-term reliability assessment is too pessimistic, including that its assumption of 160 GW of demand growth by 2030, 90 GW of it from data centres, may be overstated.
frame_summary: The piece argues the institutional reliability consensus rests on conservative assumptions, and that correcting for likely-to-connect queue resources and realistic data-centre load resolves most projected shortfalls.
verbatim_quote: NERC’s assumption that electric demand will grow by 160 GW by 2030, including 90 GW from data centers, may be overstated, according to Grid Strategies.
verbatim_list: “NERC’s 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment is too pessimistic,” Grid Strategies analysts said in the report
Data center development may be limited by supply chain shortages of chips, power transformers and other key inputs

title: Navigating safe-harbor rules for solar and wind Sec. 48E facilities
key_claim: Wind and solar facilities beginning construction after 4 July 2026 must be placed in service by 31 December 2027 to claim the Sec. 48E credit, and Notice 2025-42 restricts most projects to the physical-work test for proving construction start.
frame_summary: The article argues OBBBA and Notice 2025-42 have turned tax-credit eligibility into a construction-timeline and documentation race, layering foreign-entity sourcing tests on top of an accelerated placed-in-service cliff.
verbatim_quote: If the construction of the wind and solar facility begins after July 4, 2026, the qualified property must be placed in service by the taxpayer by Dec. 31, 2027, to qualify for the credit.
verbatim_list: Notice 2025-42 limits taxpayers’ ability to claim the start of construction began on or before July 4, 2026, for wind and solar facilities and thereby accelerates placed-in-service dates to Dec. 31, 2027

If the start of construction began on or after Jan. 1, 2026, but on or before July 4, 2026, and assuming the continuity safe-harbor provision of Notice 2022-61 is relied upon, the wind and solar facilities receive an extended placed-in-service deadline of Dec. 31, 2030.
